_note: Batch 1c — instruments, mix bus and the first concepts. 31 answers against canonical ids. The concept entries are deliberately last: they are what a producer reads once and uses forever, so they are worth writing after the practical ones have set the voice.

questions.q: Why does my distorted guitar sound harsh?
questions.short: Low-pass above 8 kHz. There is nothing but fizz up there on a distorted guitar.
steps: Low-pass at 7–9 kHz. A real cabinet rolls off here anyway, so nothing musical is lost.
Sweep 2.5–4 kHz for the ice-pick peak and cut it 3–5 dB with a narrow Q.
If it is a DI with an amp sim, change the cabinet impulse before touching EQ.
High-pass at 80–100 Hz so the low end stops fighting the bass.
questions.why: Distortion generates harmonics all the way up, but a guitar speaker physically cannot reproduce above about 6 kHz. Everything above that is an artefact of the amp sim, not part of the instrument.
questions.watch: Low-passing too low, below 6 kHz, makes the guitar sound like it is behind a door.

questions.q: How do I make my distorted guitars wider?
questions.short: Two performances hard-panned. One take widened is not wide, it is phasey.
steps: Record the part twice and pan the takes 100% left and right.
Use a different amp, cabinet or pickup on each so they differ in tone as well as timing.
Keep both dry and centred in the low end — high-pass both at 100 Hz.
Check mono: real doubles stay solid, fake ones cancel.
questions.why: Two performances differ in timing by a few milliseconds randomly across the whole part, which the ear reads as width. A delayed copy differs by a fixed amount, which it reads as a comb filter.
questions.watch: If only one take exists, use a short stereo delay rather than a widener and accept it will be narrower.

questions.q: Why does my distorted guitar sound muddy?
questions.short: High-pass at 100 Hz and cut 200–400 Hz. Guitars need no low end in a full mix.
steps: High-pass at 100–120 Hz. The bass owns everything below that.
Cut 3–4 dB at 200–400 Hz, which is where layered guitars pile up.
If two guitars play the same part, cut different bands on each.
Reduce the amp's gain before you reach for more EQ — mud is usually too much distortion.
questions.why: High-gain amps add enormous low-mid energy that sounds huge in solo. In a mix that energy is in the way of the bass, the snare and the vocal all at once.
questions.watch: Less gain almost always sounds heavier in a mix. Try that before any EQ move.

questions.q: Why does my clean electric guitar sound thin?
questions.short: Add 150–250 Hz and compress lightly. A clean DI has no amp to add body for it.
steps: Lower the high-pass to 90 Hz and lift 2 dB at 150–250 Hz.
Compress at 3:1 with 2–3 dB so the quiet notes come up to the loud ones.
Add light tube saturation to generate the harmonics an amp would have added.
Double it and pan if it is still thin — layering beats boosting here.
questions.why: A guitar amp is a distortion and EQ device as much as an amplifier. A clean DI skips all of that, which is why it sounds correct and lifeless at the same time.
questions.watch: Too much 200 Hz on a clean guitar puts it straight into the vocal's chest range.

questions.q: How do I push my clean electric guitar further back?
questions.short: Cut 2–4 kHz where the vocal lives, then add reverb. Do not just lower it.
steps: Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz, the vocal's presence band.
Add a medium reverb, 1.2–1.8 s, with a high send to place it behind.
Pan it 30–50% off centre.
Roll off above 9 kHz so it reads as further away.
questions.why: A clean guitar's pick attack sits exactly where vocal consonants do. Removing the overlap lets the guitar keep its level and its part while the words stay clear.
questions.watch: In highlife and worship the guitar figure is the hook. Check with the arrangement before pushing it back.

questions.q: Why does my acoustic guitar sound boxy?
questions.short: The mic was pointed at the sound hole. Cut 200–400 Hz and move the mic next time.
steps: Cut 3–5 dB at 200–400 Hz with a medium Q.
High-pass at 80–100 Hz to remove the body boom under it.
Add 2 dB at 6–10 kHz for the string detail the cut takes with it.
Next session, aim the mic at the twelfth fret, not the sound hole.
questions.why: The sound hole is a bass port. Everything that makes an acoustic sound boomy and boxy comes out of it, and everything that makes one sound detailed comes off the strings.
questions.watch: Cutting too much low mid makes the acoustic sound like a ukulele.

questions.q: How do I make my acoustic guitar brighter?
questions.short: Shelf above 8 kHz for string detail, and clear the low mids so the top can be heard.
steps: Cut 2 dB at 200–350 Hz first. The top end appears without boosting anything.
Add a 2–3 dB shelf above 8 kHz for string and fingernail detail.
Use a transient designer to raise attack if the picking is soft.
Avoid 3–5 kHz — that is where an acoustic gets clanky rather than bright.
questions.why: Perceived brightness is a ratio between the top end and the low mids, so removing low mids raises it just as effectively as boosting treble and costs no headroom or noise.
questions.watch: Boosting high shelf on a bright-strung acoustic brings up fret squeak as much as detail.

questions.q: Why does my acoustic guitar sound boomy?
aliases: too much low end on acoustic
questions.short: Proximity effect plus the body resonance around 100–150 Hz. Filter and notch.
steps: High-pass at 100 Hz, higher than you would for a solo recording.
Sweep 100–160 Hz for the body resonance and cut it 3–5 dB narrow.
If the mic was very close, back it off to 20–30 cm next time.
In a full band mix, high-pass as high as 150 Hz — the acoustic needs no weight there.
questions.why: Every directional microphone boosts low frequencies as it gets closer to the source, and an acoustic's own body resonance sits in the same range, so the two stack.
questions.watch: A solo acoustic recording needs that low end. Only filter this hard when there is a band underneath.

questions.q: Why does my piano sound muddy?
questions.short: The left hand is doubling the bass. Fix the arrangement before the EQ.
steps: Check whether the pianist is playing the same notes as the bass. If so, that is the problem.
High-pass the piano at 120–200 Hz in a full arrangement and let the bass own below.
Cut 2–3 dB at 250–400 Hz for the remaining buildup.
Add 1–2 dB at 2–4 kHz for note definition.
questions.why: A piano covers the entire range of every other instrument in the arrangement at once, so it overlaps everything by default. Deciding which octaves it is allowed to own does more than any EQ curve.
questions.watch: On a solo piano ballad, none of this applies. Filter only when something else needs the room.

questions.q: How do I push my piano further back?
questions.short: Narrow it, darken it, and cut the vocal's band out of it. Width is what makes it feel close.
steps: Reduce the stereo width to 50–60%; a full-width piano surrounds the listener.
Cut 2 dB at 2–4 kHz where the vocal needs presence.
Roll off above 10 kHz so it sits behind.
Add a medium hall send rather than lowering the fader.
questions.why: A wide source feels close because it occupies the space around the listener. Narrowing it is the fastest way to move something back without losing any of its level.
questions.watch: Narrowing too far makes a piano sound like a keyboard patch.

questions.q: How do I make my piano brighter?
questions.short: Shelf above 8 kHz and clear 250–400 Hz. Avoid 1–3 kHz, which makes a piano clangy.
steps: Cut 2 dB at 250–400 Hz. The clarity appears before you boost anything.
Add a 2 dB shelf above 8 kHz for hammer and string detail.
Lift 1 dB at 5 kHz only if the attack is still soft.
Leave 1–3 kHz alone unless you want a bar-room piano.
questions.why: A piano's perceived brightness comes from the hammer noise and the upper partials, both above 6 kHz. The 1–3 kHz band holds the body of the note, and boosting it reads as hard rather than bright.
questions.watch: Bright piano and bright hats in the same mix is where top-end fatigue comes from.

questions.q: Why does my organ sound muddy?
questions.short: An organ fills every gap by design. High-pass it hard and carve the band the choir needs.
steps: High-pass at 150–250 Hz. In gospel this is much higher than feels right, and it works.
Cut 3 dB at 300–500 Hz where it collides with the choir and the lead.
Sidechain the organ to duck 2 dB under the lead vocal.
Narrow it slightly; a full-width organ swallows the stereo field.
questions.why: A Hammond with drawbars out is deliberately a wall of sustained harmonics with no gaps. Everything else in the mix has to be given room by removing organ, because the organ will never stop playing.
questions.watch: Filter too high and you lose the pedal bass that holds a traditional gospel arrangement together.

questions.q: How do I push my organ further back?
questions.short: Duck it under the vocal automatically. A static balance cannot serve both.
steps: Sidechain the organ to the lead vocal, 2–3 dB, with a slow 250 ms release.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz permanently.
Keep the Leslie's top rotor but roll off above 8 kHz.
Ride the fader up in the instrumental sections so it still gets its moments.
questions.why: The organ is the instrument that fills the space when the singer stops. Ducking makes the mix do automatically what the organist does by ear in the room.
questions.watch: Fast ducking on sustained chords is audible as pumping. Keep the release long.

questions.q: How do I make my Rhodes warmer?
questions.short: Tube saturation and a gentle lift at 200–400 Hz. Resist cutting the top instead.
steps: Add tube or tape saturation before EQ — a Rhodes through a real amp is what warm means here.
Lift 1.5 dB at 200–400 Hz with a wide bell.
Add a slow chorus or tremolo at a subtle depth for movement.
Roll off above 12 kHz only if the sample is a bright digital one.
questions.why: The warmth people associate with a Rhodes is the amplifier and the tines, not the keyboard. Sampled Rhodes patches capture the note and leave the circuit behind.
questions.watch: Too much 200–400 Hz on a Rhodes puts it directly in the way of the vocal's chest.

questions.q: Why does my Rhodes disappear in the mix?
questions.short: It is in the same band as everything else. Give it the 1–2 kHz bell nothing else uses.
steps: Lift 2 dB at 1–2 kHz for the tine attack, and cut the same band on the guitars.
High-pass at 120 Hz so it stops competing with the bass.
Widen it slightly so it occupies space the centre instruments do not.
Automate it up 2 dB in the gaps between vocal phrases.
questions.why: A Rhodes is a mid-range instrument with a soft attack, so it has neither the low end nor the transient that normally lets something cut through. Its tine click at 1–2 kHz is the only distinctive thing it has.
questions.watch: Lifting 1–2 kHz too far makes a Rhodes sound like an electric piano preset.

questions.q: Why does my synth lead sound harsh?
questions.short: Change the patch before you EQ it. A harsh saw is harsh at the oscillator, not the output.
steps: Lower the filter cutoff or reduce resonance at the synth itself.
Then cut 3–4 dB at 2–5 kHz with a dynamic EQ so it only engages on the loud notes.
Low-pass above 12 kHz; digital synths generate content no speaker needs.
Add tape saturation, which rounds the edges of a hard digital waveform.
questions.why: A synth is the one source where you can fix the recording after the fact. Editing the patch solves at the source what EQ can only mask at the output.
questions.watch: Dulling a lead too far leaves it inaudible against bright hats and vocals.

questions.q: How do I make my synth lead wider?
questions.short: Detune two oscillators and pan them, rather than putting a widener on the output.
steps: Use two oscillators detuned 8–15 cents and pan them opposite inside the synth.
Add a stereo delay of 12–25 ms on one side only if you need more.
Keep everything below 150 Hz mono.
Check mono — detuned unison survives it, a widener usually does not.
questions.why: Detuning creates genuine differences between the channels at every frequency, which is what real width is. A widener fabricates that difference with phase tricks that undo themselves in mono.
questions.watch: Heavy unison detune makes a lead sound out of tune against a piano or horns.

questions.q: How do I push my pad further back?
questions.short: A pad belongs under everything. Filter both ends hard and duck it under the vocal.
steps: High-pass at 200–300 Hz and low-pass at 8–10 kHz. A pad lives in the middle.
Sidechain it to the lead vocal, 3–4 dB, slow release.
Cut 3 dB at 2–4 kHz permanently.
Lower it until you only notice when it is muted — that is the correct level.
questions.why: A pad's job is to make a mix feel full without being heard, so the test is not whether it sounds good but whether removing it sounds worse. Filtering both ends leaves only the part that does that job.
questions.watch: Filtering both ends too hard leaves a thin band that sounds like a telephone.

questions.q: Why does my pad sound muddy?
questions.short: It is sustained, so even a small low-mid lift never stops. High-pass higher than feels right.
steps: High-pass at 250–350 Hz. On a sustained source this is normal, not extreme.
Cut 3 dB at 300–500 Hz on top of the filter.
Narrow the low end to mono even after filtering.
If it is a stacked patch, remove one layer instead of EQing the sum.
questions.why: Transient sources contribute low-mid energy in short bursts the ear forgives. A pad holds the same energy continuously, so it is the single most common cause of a mix that is muddy for its whole duration.
questions.watch: Filtering a pad this high can remove the chord's root. Check it still implies the harmony.

questions.q: How do I make my strings wider?
questions.short: Pan by section, as an orchestra sits. Violins left, cellos right, not one wide patch.
steps: Split the arrangement into separate violin, viola and cello parts.
Pan them as they sit in a real section: high strings left, low strings right.
Use one hall reverb across the whole group so they share a space.
Vary each part's timing by a few milliseconds so they are not perfectly locked.
questions.why: A sampled string patch is already a wide stereo recording, so widening it further only exaggerates something fake. Splitting the parts and placing them is what makes sampled strings sound like players.
questions.watch: One shared reverb is what glues the sections. Separate reverbs make them sound like separate recordings.

questions.q: Why do my strings sound harsh?
questions.short: Cut 2–4 kHz dynamically. Sampled strings have a bow-noise peak that never varies.
steps: Sweep 2–4 kHz, find the bow peak, and cut it 3–4 dB with dynamic EQ.
Lower the velocity of the loudest passages rather than compressing them.
Add a hall reverb; dry strings are always harsher than wet ones.
Use a warmer articulation in the sampler before you EQ anything.
questions.why: Real strings are almost always heard in a hall, where the room softens the bow noise before it reaches you. A dry sampled string section is an instrument nobody has ever heard in life.
questions.watch: Cutting the bow noise entirely makes strings sound synthetic. Reduce it, do not remove it.

questions.q: How do I glue my horns together?
questions.short: One bus, one compressor, one reverb. A horn section is one instrument, not four.
steps: Route every horn to one bus and do all the processing there.
Compress the bus at 4:1 with 3–5 dB so they breathe together.
Give the bus one room or plate reverb, never one per player.
Pan them as they would stand: trumpets out, trombones and sax nearer centre.
questions.why: A real horn section plays into the same room air and their dynamics move together. Bus compression and a shared reverb reproduce both of those, which is why it works where individual processing never does.
questions.watch: Bus compression pulls up the breath and key noise on every horn at once.

questions.q: Why do my horns sound harsh?
questions.short: Cut 2–5 kHz on the bus dynamically. Horns are harsh only on the loud notes.
steps: Use dynamic EQ at 2–5 kHz on the horn bus, cutting 3–5 dB on peaks only.
Slow the compressor attack to 15–20 ms so it stops clamping the body.
Add a room reverb; horns recorded dry always sound harsh.
Check mic placement next time — off-axis is warmer for brass.
questions.why: Brass gets brighter the louder it is played, so the harshness only exists in the loudest bars. A static cut makes the quiet passages dull to solve a problem they do not have.
questions.watch: Dulling horns too far removes the brightness that makes a section sound triumphant.

questions.q: How do I get my mix loud without squashing it?
aliases: my mix is not loud enough
mix clips when I push it
questions.short: Loudness is won in the balance, not on the limiter. Fix the low end before you push.
steps: Cut 2–3 dB at 200–400 Hz across the mix. Low-mid buildup is what eats loudness.
Clip the loudest drum transients 2–3 dB before the limiter ever sees them.
Then limit 3–4 dB, not 8. If you need more, go back to the balance.
Check against a reference at matched loudness, not matched fader.
questions.why: A limiter reduces the loudest peaks, so a mix with one source 4 dB too loud will limit that source and nothing else. Balance determines how much loudness is available before the limiter is even inserted.
questions.watch: Streaming normalises everything to around −14 LUFS anyway, so past a point you are only losing dynamics.

questions.q: How do I make my mix wider?
questions.short: Width is an arrangement decision. Pan the parts; do not widen the master.
steps: Pan the individual parts first. Most narrow mixes are narrow because everything is centred.
Keep kick, snare, bass and lead vocal in the centre. Everything else can move.
If you must widen the bus, use mid/side above 300 Hz only, 1–2 dB.
Check mono after every change.
questions.why: A stereo widener on the master cannot create information that is not in the recording; it can only exaggerate the difference between channels, which is also what makes a mix collapse in mono.
questions.watch: Club and phone playback are effectively mono. A mix that only works wide does not work.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound harsh?
questions.short: Find the one source causing it. A cut on the bus dulls everything to fix one channel.
steps: Solo each source in turn with the 2–5 kHz band boosted, and find the offender.
Fix it on that channel: usually hats, a synth, or an over-compressed vocal.
If three or more sources share it, then and only then cut 1 dB on the bus.
Check your monitoring level — mixing loud makes you add treble you do not need.
questions.why: Harshness is additive across sources but each one contributes a small amount, so the bus shows a problem that exists nowhere in particular. Cutting on the bus treats every source for one source's fault.
questions.watch: A mix that sounds harsh only after an hour is ear fatigue, not the mix. Take a break and re-check.

questions.q: Why is my mix pumping?
aliases: compression is pumping on my mix
questions.short: The kick is driving the bus compressor's detector. Filter the sidechain at 100 Hz.
steps: High-pass the bus compressor's sidechain at 80–120 Hz so the kick stops triggering it.
Lower the ratio to 1.5:1 or 2:1 and aim for 1–2 dB of gain reduction only.
Set the release so the meter recovers before the next beat.
Check whether the limiter, not the compressor, is doing the pumping.
questions.why: The kick has far more energy than anything else, so an unfiltered detector hears mostly kick and ducks the entire mix on every beat. Filtering the sidechain lets the compressor respond to the music instead.
questions.watch: Some pumping is the sound of a record. Decide whether you are fixing a fault or removing a feature.

questions.q: How do I make my whole mix hit harder?
questions.short: Punch is contrast. If everything is loud all the time, nothing can hit.
steps: Lower the sustained elements — pads, organ, reverb returns — by 1–2 dB.
Slow every attack time on the drum bus so transients survive.
Check the limiter is not flattening the transients you just protected.
Mute one element entirely. Punch usually appears when something leaves.
questions.why: The ear reads punch as the difference between the transient and what surrounds it. Raising the transient is one way to increase that difference; lowering everything else is the way that costs no headroom.
questions.watch: A mix that is punchy and quiet is better than one that is loud and flat. Judge at matched loudness.

questions.q: What is gain staging and why does it matter?
aliases: how loud should my tracks be
questions.short: Set every channel to peak around −12 dBFS so plugins and your ears both work in their happy range.
steps: Aim each channel at −18 to −12 dBFS average, with peaks no higher than −6.
Use clip gain or a trim plugin at the top of the chain, not the fader.
Check the master is not clipping before you add a single plugin.
Re-check after any plugin that adds level, which is most of them.
questions.why: Analogue-modelled plugins change their behaviour with input level, and a channel hitting 0 dBFS leaves no room for the summing to work. Setting levels low once at the start removes a whole class of problems you would otherwise chase all mix.
questions.watch: Digital headroom is free but your monitor level is not. Turn the speakers up, not the faders.

questions.q: What LUFS should I master to?
aliases: what loudness should I master to
questions.short: −14 LUFS for streaming, −9 to −7 for club, −23 for broadcast. Mix for the song, not the number.
steps: Streaming (Spotify, Apple, YouTube, Tidal): target −14 LUFS integrated, true peak −1 dBTP.
Club or DJ playback: −9 to −7 LUFS, because PA systems do not normalise.
Broadcast under EBU R128: −23 LUFS, with half a unit of tolerance.
Measure integrated across the whole song, not over the loudest chorus.
questions.why: Streaming platforms turn everything down to a common loudness, so a master at −6 LUFS is played at the same volume as one at −14 and has simply lost its dynamics on the way. The number is a ceiling for your own benefit, not a competition.
questions.watch: True peak matters more than LUFS for audio quality. Leave −1 dBTP so lossy encoding does not clip.

questions.q: What is parallel compression?
questions.short: Compress a copy to destruction, then blend it under the dry signal. Density without losing the hits.
steps: Send the source to a bus and compress it hard: 10:1, fast attack, 10–20 dB of gain reduction.
Bring that bus up underneath the dry channel until you hear it, then back it off slightly.
EQ the parallel bus separately — high-pass it so it adds body, not mud.
Check phase: if the blend thins the source, something is delaying one path.
questions.why: Compression raises the quiet parts and lowers the loud ones. Mixing a heavily compressed copy under the original raises the quiet parts without ever touching the peaks, so you gain density while the transients stay exactly as they were.
questions.watch: Any latency difference between the two paths causes comb filtering. Use plugin delay compensation.
